title: The Mouse, the Bird, and the Sausage
paragraphs: Once upon a time a mouse, a bird and a sausage went into partnership and set up house together. For a long while everything went well. They lived comfortably and did so well that their stores grew considerably. The bird’s job was to fly into the woods every day and bring back firewood. The mouse fetched the water, and the sausage did the cooking.

When people are too well off, they always start longing for something new. So it happened that the bird, out one day, met another bird and boasted to him at length about how well their household was run. But the other bird sneered at him for being a poor fool who did all the hard work while the other two stayed home and had an easy time. After all, once the mouse had lit the fire and fetched the water, she could retire to her little room and rest until it was time to lay the table. The sausage only had to watch the pot and make sure the food was cooking properly, and when dinnertime was near, he would throw himself into the broth, or roll in and out among the vegetables three or four times, and there they were, buttered and salted and ready to serve. Then, when the bird came home and put down his load, they sat down to eat, and when the meal was over they could sleep as much as they liked until the next morning. It really was a very pleasant life.

Swayed by these remarks, the bird refused the next morning to bring in the wood. He told the others that he had been their servant long enough, and a fool besides, and that it was time for a change, to try arranging the work some other way. The mouse and the sausage begged and pleaded, but it did no good. The bird stayed firm, and the experiment had to be made. So they drew lots, and it fell to the sausage to bring the wood, to the mouse to cook, and to the bird to fetch the water.

And what happened then? The sausage set off to look for wood, the bird made the fire, and the mouse put the pot on, and the two of them waited for the sausage to come back with fuel for the next day. But the sausage stayed away so long that they grew worried, and the bird flew out to meet him. He hadn’t flown far when he came upon a dog. The dog had met the sausage, taken him for fair game, and seized him and swallowed him. The bird complained to the dog about this barefaced robbery, but nothing he said made any difference. The dog replied that he had found forged papers on the sausage, and that was why he had forfeited his life.
The bird picked up the wood and flew home sadly, and told the mouse everything he had seen and heard. They were both very unhappy, but they agreed to make the best of it and stay together.

So now the bird laid the table, and the mouse looked after the food. Wanting to prepare it the way the sausage had, by rolling in and out among the vegetables to salt and butter them, she jumped into the pot. But she stopped short long before she reached the bottom, having already lost not just her skin and hair, but her life as well.

Soon the bird came in, ready to serve the dinner, but he couldn’t find the cook anywhere. In his alarm and confusion he flung the wood about the floor, calling and searching, but no cook was to be found. Then some of the wood he had carelessly thrown down caught fire and began to blaze. The bird rushed to fetch water, but his bucket fell into the well, and he fell in after it, and since he could not get himself out, he drowned.
